entries.title: Three men shot in South Lawndale, two hours after another man shot blocks away
entries.summary: <p>Three people were shot blocks from the Cook County Criminal Courthouse Tuesday evening, according to Chicago police.</p><p>Someone inside a tan sedan fired shots, striking three men in the 2400 block of South Washtenaw Avenue at 8:44 p.m., police said.</p><p>A 21-year-old was shot in the head and taken to Stroger Hospital in serious condition, police said. A 27-year-old man was shot in the head and listed in critical condition, and a 22-year-old was shot in the leg and was listed in good condition; both were taken to Mt. Sinai Hospital.</p><p>About two hours earlier, another man was shot in the 2700 block of West 25th Street at 6:33 p.m. while standing in front of a home, police said. He was taken to Mt. Sinai Hospital in good condition.</p><p>No one is in custody related to either shooting, police said.</p>

entries.title: CBS' '60 minutes' announces new slate of correspondents for upcoming season
entries.summary: <p>NEW YORK — Two months after a major shakeup, CBS’s “60 Minutes” has hired a lineup of new correspondents and contributors in time for its 59th season, including Ross Douthat, a conservative opinion columnist at The New York Times, and Norah O'Donnell, former anchor of “CBS Evening News.”</p><p>The show's new executive producer, Nick Bilton, announced the news in a staff memo Tuesday, shared on X. Joining Douthat and O'Donnell will be author Sebastian Junger, Trevor Phillips and Gianna Toboni. All will be contributors to the show.</p><p>The new journalists join current correspondents Lesley Stahl, Jon Wertheim and Bill Whitaker. Their hirings come two months after a shakeup at the storied program, led by the network's new editor-in-chief, Bari Weiss.</p><p>Weiss installed Bilton, who has little substantive broadcast news experience, as executive producer, replacing Tanya Simon, who was let go after a 30-plus year tenure with the show. Also let go were correspondents Sharyn Alfonsi and Cecilia Vega — and soon after, Scott Pelley, after a tense confrontation with his bosses over the changes.</p><p>In addition to the three dismissed, Anderson Cooper — whose primary job is at CNN — said earlier this year he was leaving of his own accord after two decades.</p><h3>CBS News leaders enthused about the hires</h3><p>Weiss and Tom Cibrowski, the CBS News president, praised the new hires in an internal memo. “We couldn’t be more excited about this news,” the two said, welcoming the new additions. “Onward!”</p><p>Bilton called Douthat “one of the preeminent public intellectuals in America today, a thinker of uncommon rigor and a journalist of deep empathy.” The columnist has spent nearly two decades at the Times and is an author of numerous books.</p><p>The producer called O’Donnell “a powerhouse.”</p><p>“You’ve seen her all over the network. She’s launched a new podcast. And you’ll see much more of her in our halls because Norah will be a correspondent on 60 Minutes."</p><p>Bilton praised Junger for his nonfiction work “The Perfect Storm,” about a catastrophic 1991 storm. The book “landed with an electric charge in the world of reported nonfiction, defining an intense and intimate form of storytelling and establishing Sebastian as a generational talent,” Bilton said.</p><p>Toboni joins “60 Minutes” as a contributor and CBS News as a national correspondent. Previously a senior correspondent with VICE News and VICE on HBO, she comes to the program from CNN.</p><p>Calling her a journalist of “extraordinary range,” Bilton noted that Toboni has interviewed members of ISIS, investigated cartel violence in Mexico and has written a book on the death penalty.</p><p>Also serving as contributor will be Trevor Phillips, announced last month as the news division's senior global affairs correspondent. Based in London, he is “one of the most respected and trusted voices in the United Kingdom for his ability to ask the toughest questions and hold anyone in power to account,” Bilton wrote in his memo.</p><h3>‘60 Minutes’ has faced upheaval for a while</h3><p>Turmoil had raged at “60 Minutes” for more than a year before the May shakeup. Much of it came after President Donald Trump sued the show over its editing of a 2024 interview with then-Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris.</p><p>That became part of a broader shakeup at CBS News after Weiss was named to the new role of editor-in-chief by parent company Paramount late last year following David Ellison’s arrival as the network’s corporate leader.</p>

entries.title: Bomb threat cleared at Evanston hospital
entries.summary: <p>Police gave the all clear Tuesday after a suspicious package found outside Endeavor Health Evanston Hospital prompted the building to be locked down for a bomb threat investigation.</p><p>Officials closed the hospital around 5:30 p.m. and deployed a drone to survey the “suspicious package with wires protruding from it," Evanston police said in a statement. The Cook County Bomb Squad was also on the scene.</p><p>The area around the hospital was reopened around 8:10 p.m. after the package was determined not to be a threat, police said.</p>

entries.title: 4 tornadoes hit Chicago area during Monday's storms, officials say
entries.summary: <p>People across the greater Chicago area on Tuesday were dealing with the effects of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/07/27/weather-storms-heat-wind" target="_blank" >heavy thunderstorms</a> and four confirmed tornadoes from the day before.</p><p>A clear, sunny day brought some relief, as floodwaters receded, basements could at least start to dry out, damages were assessed and power was being restored across the region.</p><p>Officials said the communities hit hardest during Monday’s storm include Chicago Heights, Maywood, Crestwood, Bolingbrook, University Park, Libertyville and portions of the South Side.</p><p>The four tornadoes touched down in the south and west suburbs, survey teams with the National Weather Service confirmed Tuesday afternoon and evening. </p><p>One tornado hit south suburban Lansing, while another passed through south suburban Country Club Hills, Hazel Crest, Harvey and Homewood. Both tornadoes had gusts topping 110 mph, according to the weather service.</p><p>The other two tornadoes hit west suburban Glen Ellyn and south suburban Orland Park, each with winds reaching a max of 85 mph, according to the weather service.</p><p>Big wind gusts were recorded elsewhere across the city and suburbs, topping out at 82 mph recorded in Waukegan, according to the weather service. Midway Airport recorded winds of 73 mph, and O’Hare Airport saw 65 mph winds.</p><p>The weather service said it also confirmed damaging straight line winds in Carol Stream and Downers Grove, and that surveyors would continue to assess the damage across the region.</p><p>Besides the damaging wind, the downpour flooded hundreds of basements.</p><p>Chicago reported at least 599 flooded homes, according to the city’s Office of Emergency Management and Communications. Among Chicago’s wards, the one with the most reports of flooded basements was the 8th Ward on the Far South Side.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-750000" name="html-embed-module-750000"></a><div style="min-height:918px" id="datawrapper-vis-SXryo"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/SXryo/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-SXryo"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/SXryo/full.png" alt="Across the city, Chicagoans called in thousands of times to 311 due to yesterday's storms (Choropleth map)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>In some pockets of Cook County those 2 inches of rain fell in just two hours, according to the Metropolitan Water Reclamation District.</p><p>The heavy rain overwhelmed some streets and drainage systems. Chicago’s official climate station at O’Hare measured 1.76 inches, while Midway received 2.94 inches. Much of the Chicago area saw 2 to 4 inches of rain.</p><p>The two major reservoirs managing that rainfall both are filling, with one nearing capacity <a class="Link" href="https://mwrd.org/" target="_blank" >according to the MWRD</a>, with McCook Reservoir about 93% full, storing about 4.8 billion gallons. The Thornton Reservoir, to the south, is about 42% full, storing nearly 3.6 billion gallons.</p><p>In Downers Grove, meanwhile, crews on Tuesday <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/07/28/downers-grove-sewer-storm-drain" target="_blank" >recovered the body</a> of a contractor trapped in a Downers Grove storm drain during the storm.</p><p>Besides all those flooded basements, Chicago also reported receiving 2,322 calls about trees that were down or damaged, and 973 reports of tree debris. Add that to the roughly 40,000 requests for service involving downed or damaged trees, or tree debris, the city received from June 10 through July 7, when several intense storms hit the city.</p><p>Chicago officials also said the recent storm led to 623 reports of water on streets and 47 flooded viaducts around Chicago as well as 310 traffic signals out; 220 streetlights out; 160 downed wires; and 116 damaged streetlight poles as of Tuesday afternoon.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-7e0000" name="html-embed-module-7e0000"></a><div style="min-height:606px" id="datawrapper-vis-pDMHz"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/pDMHz/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-pDMHz"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/pDMHz/full.png" alt="As yesterday's storm rolled in, Chicagoans placed thousands of calls to the city's 311 hotline (Area Chart)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>According to ComEd, more than 530,000 customers lost power as a result of the storm. By Tuesday morning, crews had restored electricity to nearly 300,000 customers, according to ComEd. The utility expects that by noon Wednesday it will have restored power to about 80% of those who lost their electricity. The rest of ComEd customers will have power restored by 10 p.m. Friday, according to the utility.</p><p>In south suburban Crete, Kristin Webster said she heard wind and rain whipping through her neighborhood Monday afternoon. By the time the storm passed, much of the village lost power, and for Webster, it still hasn’t been restored. </p><p>Webster, 46, observed several downed trees in the area, including two that crushed her neighbors’ cars. But the most frustrating part of dealing with the storm’s aftermath has been how long it’s been since the initial damage.</p><p>“Nobody should be put in the situation where they can't have the normal comforts of home, especially 30 hours later,” she told the Chicago Sun-Times. “I've never seen anything like this.”</p><p>Webster said she anticipates throwing away refrigerated food that will go bad before power is restored, and she plans to drive 40 minutes south to a friend’s home that has power in order to refrigerate some medication.</p><p>In a post on social media, ComEd acknowledged the frustration people without power are facing, but said the severe weather is nearly unprecedented, and it will take time to restore power to everyone.</p><p>“When storms cause this level of damage across dozens of communities at the same time, restoration becomes significantly more complex,” the post reads.</p><p></p><p>Additionally, AT&T has reported wireless disruptions primarily within Cook and DuPage counties. An AT&T spokesperson said “we are working as quickly and safely as possible to restore service.”</p><p>The Illinois American Red Cross has also opened two shelters, in Steger and Gurnee, to help those affected by the storm. According to regional communications director Connie Esparza, many Illinoisans have come to the shelter for access to electricity and food, with some staying overnight.</p><p>As cleanup efforts continue, officials are urging residents to avoid downed power lines, report hazards and use caution while traveling through areas still affected by flooding, fallen trees and power outages.</p>

entries.title: Is injured White Sox catcher Kyle Teel catching with a walking boot?
entries.summary: <p>As reporters sat in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox’</a> dugout waiting for manager Will Venable to speak Tuesday, injured catcher Kyle Teel emerged from the tunnel connected to the clubhouse dressed in full gear: mask, chest protector and shin guards. He was only eight days removed from suffering a high sprain of his left ankle and had been seen wearing a walking boot the night before.</p><p>Was this a miraculous recovery from an injury that’s expected to shelve Teel for six to 12 weeks?</p><p>As it turned out, no, it wasn’t. As Teel walked past the assembled media, his walking boot became visible after being hidden by the shin guard. But it was a sight not seen before. Oblivious to the watchful eyes, Teel walked through the dugout and headed to the bullpen, where he caught light baseballs while seated or kneeling in an effort to stay sharp.</p><p>“I wasn’t aware that was part of the plan today,” Venable said. “If [trainer James Kruk] is OK with it, I’m sure it’s fine.”</p><p>Venable said that nothing has changed regarding Teel’s timetable and that he hasn’t done any baseball activities since the injury — at least until Tuesday.</p><p>“That’s the first,” Venable said. “He’s been really stationary to this point.”</p><p>It’s evidence of Teel’s work ethic and perhaps his FOMO (fear of missing out, for those unfamiliar with the acronym). But the Sox don’t want him pushing his limits.</p><p>“There’s always that back and forth between the player and the training staff,” Venable said. “Really a collaboration in trying to figure out what’s the right amount to push or when and how to go about it. Unfortunately with these injuries, he’s learning how to go about his treatment and handle it the right way.</p><p>“No update other than Kyle is going about this with a really positive attitude and doing a great job of getting his work in. And obviously with a boot on, still finding ways to get work in and get his treatment in, as well.”</p><h3>Maddon’s influence</h3><p>Venable learned a lot as a base coach under former Cubs manager Joe Maddon from 2018 to 2020. One of those lessons was to have few team meetings. But as the Sox’ manager, Venable has put his own spin on it, hosting what he calls “state of the Sox” meetings monthly.</p><p>“I address the team, and we just open the floor to talk about things,” Venable said. “That’s the time where if there are broader issues to discuss, we’ll talk about those things.</p><p>“Joe Maddon would meet with the team three times a year; would never ever do other kinds of meetings. There’s something about that that I liked. Not rigid about it, but just want to have a routine that they know we’re going to get together and talk.”</p><p>One topic at the next meeting might be the trade deadline, which is at 5 p.m. Monday. That can be a distraction for everyone and could be worth discussing.</p><p>“Rarely do the players have stuff. It happens every once in a while,” Venable said. “It’s in the spirit of being proactive and not having a team meeting in response to a thing and just creating a platform for guys if they have something. They haven’t been that heavy, to be honest.”</p><h3>Challenging challenges</h3><p>When the Sox used — and lost — both of their pitch challenges in the first inning Sunday, Steve Stone offered biting analysis on the Chicago Sports Network broadcast: “Not a great plan.”</p><p>Indeed not. But Venable doesn’t want the Sox leaving a game with unused challenges. He wants his players to be aggressive with them. How aggressive is still being determined.</p><p>“It’s been real challenging to find the right tone and guidelines to put in place,” Venable said. “You want to support and empower them to use this as a tool that can help swing an at-bat, can swing a game. And at the same time, there’s times where it’s not great to challenge if you’re not sure.”</p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" entries.title: American Airlines flights grounded nationwide for tech issue
entries.summary: <p>A “technology issue” grounded American Airlines flights across the country on Tuesday, according to the company.</p><p>It was unclear how many flights at Chicago’s airports were impacted, with average delays sitting around a half hour. A ground stop was temporarily issued by the Federal Aviation Administration just for the airline.</p><p>“Systems are coming back online now and flights are departing again,” the company said on social media. “We apologize to our customers for the inconvenience.”</p><p>At O’Hare Airport, more than 1,000 flights had been canceled in the last 24 hours — with nearly 600 facing more than 45 minutes of delays — while 267 had been canceled. At Midway, 222 flights were delayed, the majority of which being less than half an hour, with 13 total cancellations.<br></p>

entries.title: Crews recover body of second contractor trapped in Downers Grove sewer during storm
entries.summary: <p>The body of a contractor trapped in a Downers Grove storm drain was recovered on Tuesday, a day after two workers went missing as storms moved through the area.</p><p>Crews recovered the body around 5 p.m., town officials said on social media, more than a day after they rescued the other employee from the sewer drain.</p><p>The worker's identity has not been released. The DuPage County coroner’s office was determining the cause and manner of death, town officials said.</p><p>The rescue effort began around 12:50 p.m. Monday, when a Vortex employee flagged down Downers Grove police officers in the 800 block of Curtiss Street, town officials said. The employee told police that two workers were trapped in the storm drains. Downers Grove firefighters later arrived to perform a rescue.</p><p>Two hours later, firefighters rescued one of the workers about 200 feet down the drain, officials said. He was taken to Good Samaritan Hospital in good condition.</p><p>The second worker was found dead Tuesday in the storm sewer near Washington Street, officials said.</p><p>Officials said the man worked for the Houston, Texas-based Vortex Lining Systems LLC. </p><p>"We are devastated by the loss of our team member following an unexpected major rain event, and are doing everything we can to support his family during this incredibly difficult time," the company said in a statement. "We thank rescue crew members and first responders for their tremendous efforts."</p><p>The Occupational Safety and Health Administration was investigating the incident.</p><p>The employees had been working on a large-diameter pipe rehabilitation project to help maintain an 11-foot diameter, 2,200 foot long pipe installed in the 1960s that carries water from the St Joseph Creek to downtown Downers Grove. The project, begun last year, is set to be completed by the end of 2027.</p>

entries.title: Cubs, already strong, eye getting even better at trade deadline: ‘Hopefully we get everything we want’
entries.summary: <p>ST. LOUIS — While <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> players lamented <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/27/cubs-jameson-taillon-dfa-mlb-trade-deadline-pitching-jed-hoyer-craig-counsell-rotation" >the departure of veteran pitcher <b>Jameson Taillon</b></a> on Monday, they weren’t naive about any supposed blindside.</p><p>They know this sort of thing can happen in this game, particularly when the stakes are as high as they are for this Cubs team.</p><p>In the thick of a playoff race and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/25/cubs-playoffs-brewers-pirates-nl-central-matthew-boyd-starting-rotation" >chasing the division-leading Brewers</a> in the NL Central, the Cubs’ championship-level aspirations rest on what happens the next few months.</p><p>That starts with <b>Jed Hoyer</b>’s front office getting <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/22/cubs-mlb-trade-deadline-rumors-jed-hoyer-pitching-nico-hoerner-buyers-nl-central-standings-brewers" >a last shot at tweaking the roster</a> at the trade deadline, with the intent of best positioning these Cubs for a deep October run.</p><p>“You remove the personal stuff as much as you can,” second baseman <b>Nico Hoerner</b> said Monday. “It’s always their job to put the best possible team they can on the field.</p><p>“Absolutely, there’s urgency. These games go by fast, and the season gets short. We have a lot of really exciting things ahead of us.”</p><p>Believing in the capability of the position-player group, Hoyer & Co. will be <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/17/cubs-mlb-trade-deadline-rumors-starting-pitching-jed-hoyer-front-office" >fixating on pitching improvements</a> ahead of Monday’s deadline, attempting to strengthen an area of the roster where the depth has been tested by injuries and, in Taillon’s case, underperformance.</p><p>Though <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/16/cubs-second-half-preview-brewers-nl-central-standings-pete-crow-armstrong-mvp-craig-counsell-jed-hoyer-mlb-trade-deadline-alex-bregman" >the Cubs have earned justified plaudits</a> for weathering all those injuries and a monthlong slump to own one of the best records in baseball, going from good to great to even better by winning the trade-deadline arms race can be the difference come October.</p><p>“Our group has some pretty special things about it,” Hoerner said. “We’re not perfect, and we’re in a place now where we can definitely make some improvements to a team that’s already really strong.</p><p>“The time leading up to the trade deadline does feel different. It’s exciting. It’s an opportunity.”</p><p>Veterans of their depth being tested this year — and of that depth proving an issue during last year’s briefer-than-hoped playoff stay — the Cubs are simultaneously excited by who they already have and who they might add, the benefits of setting the front office up to buy at this time of year.</p><p>Will Hoyer’s work be enough for the Cubs to catch the Brewers or play deep into October? Time will tell.</p><p>“We want to be in this spot,” third baseman <b>Alex Bregman</b> said. “We want to be contending this time of year and making our team better and better. The guys in this room have done a good job of getting us to where we need to be.</p><p>“Hopefully we get everything we want.”</p><h3><b>Best Happ play ever?</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Left fielder <b>Ian Happ</b>’s throw to cut down a runner trying to advance to second on a hit off the wall in the eighth inning Monday deserved its highlight-reel status.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">IAN HAPP IS PUTTING ON A DEFENSIVE CLINIC. <a href="https://t.co/pIgQGYrUB6">pic.twitter.com/pIgQGYrUB6</a></p>— Chicago Cubs (@Cubs) <a href="https://x.com/Cubs/status/2081951916473393456?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">July 28, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p></p><p>But just how high does it rank on the all-time great-plays list for the four-time Gold Glover?</p><p>“I told Ian that’s the best defensive play I’ve seen him make in the three years I’ve been here,” manager <b>Craig Counsell</b> said. “I thought it was an incredible play.”</p><p>“We’ve thrown out a lot of guys together on balls down the line,” said Hoerner, who applied the tag at second base, “but off the wall like that is pretty rare and tough to do.”</p><h3><b>Bats are boomin’</b></h3><p>The Cubs’ offense stayed scorching in Tuesday’s 10-2 win over the Cardinals. They’ve scored 35 runs in their last four games, an average of 8.8 runs per contest.</p><p>The Cubs came into Tuesday third in baseball in runs scored, with 548, then added on by double digits.</p><p>“It was pretty relentless,” said left fielder <b>Ian Happ</b>, who doubled twice. “We have so many good players in this lineup that play every day, and I have all the confidence in the world this group is going to put up those kinds of numbers because that’s who we are.”</p><h3><b>Hoerner’s hot</b></h3><h3></h3><p>After collecting five hits in the first two games of the Cubs' series against the Cardinals, Hoerner is batting .417 with 12 RBIs in 11 games since the All-Star break.</p><p>“I’ve hit a good amount of line drives, that’s always a good thing. When I’m at my best, I’m hitting balls all over the field,” Hoerner said. “I’ve gotten some balls to fall that weren’t hit the hardest, which always helps.”</p><p></p><bsp-listcarousel entries.title: Illinois football coach Bret Bielema is bullish on the Big Ten
entries.summary: <p>With Jim Harbaugh long gone to the NFL, the Big Ten Media Days don’t have quite the same edge. When the three-day event kicked off at the Hilton Chicago on Tuesday, there was a lot of inside-football talk about 3-3-5 defenses and plenty of coach-speak about leadership and cohesion.</p><p>But there also was substantive discussion of some of the storm clouds hovering over college sports in general and football in particular. And as usual, there were a few zingers from Illinois coach Bret Bielema.</p><p>He didn’t wait long to take a shot at the SEC, which has been going back-and-forth with the Big Ten about which is the best football conference.</p><p>“They want to live in 2005 forever,” Bielema said.</p><p>He’s qualified to talk about the two leagues, having been a coach in both with stints at Wisconsin and Illinois wrapped around a forgettable stint at Arkansas.</p><p>A follow-up question on his SEC hot take led to Bielema weighing in on the Big Ten’s much-maligned and long-gone division names: Leaders and Legends.</p><p>“I don’t know how the hell we got there,” Bielema said, echoing the feelings of most fans and the rest of the college football world.</p><p>Wondering how he got to talking about the names of almost forgotten divisions? It was part of a story about the need to turn the page, which he clearly believes the SEC should do.</p><p>Bielema recalled his unhappiness about Wisconsin not getting the same respect as some traditional powers when the divisions were created. He vented to longtime Wisconsin coach-turned-athletic director Barry Alvarez, who told him: “Don’t worry about things you can’t control. You can’t change people’s 50 years of history in the way they think.”</p><p>It was another way of saying that was then and this is now. The Big Ten has produced the last three national champions — won by three different schools — meaning the SEC has to come up with another argument for its supposed superiority.</p><p>That argument, which former Alabama coach Nick Saban and others have been peddling lately, boils down to the SEC being a deeper conference.</p><p>Big Ten commissioner Tony Petitti pushed back hard against that narrative.</p><p>“The idea that the middle of our conference isn’t hard is just not right,” Petitti said. “At the end of the day, our teams are ready for the CFP. Our travel looks like the CFP travel. You’re going all over the country. The difficulty [of winning] on the road in the Big Ten — I just think that’s overlooked.”</p><p>Which conference plays better football is a fun argument. A more serious discussion is whether and how college sports can remain sustainable as more and more money pours into some programs and not to others.</p><p>“I don’t think you’ll talk to an AD or even a coach or anybody in the country that will tell you that exponential growth, every portal, is the right model,” Petitti said.</p><p>“We need to get to a place where we can have a model of growth that’s more realistic and looks more like what our revenue growth could possibly be.”</p><p>Part of the revenue piece is the eventual size of the playoff, which the Big Ten wants to see go from 12 teams to 24. More CFP games would mean more money. But some of that would just cancel out what the Big Ten would lose by killing its championship game — which almost certainly would happen with an expanded playoff, Pettiti said.</p><p>The spiraling costs of staying competitive in college sports and what role the federal government might have in regulating it are new — and urgent — topics.</p><p>But fans can be forgiven for wanting to return to the days when the biggest question was which conference was king.</p>
